item.title: What a /24 subnet actually means (and how to plan yours)
item.description: The /24 after an address says which part names the network and which part names the device. Here is what that means in practice, why one flat /24 is the trap, and how the books plan one /24 per zone with a static route and a firewall between them.
item.content:encoded:
Every example network in the books is written the same way: 192.168.10.0/24 for the house LAN, 10.30.0.0/24 for servers, 192.168.30.0/24 for IoT. That little /24 shows up on firewall interfaces, container network settings and VPN configs, and once you can read it, a lot of homelab networking stops being magic.

What the /24 tells you

An address like 192.168.30.57/24 has two parts. With a /24, the first three numbers (192.168.30) name the network, and the last number (.57) names the device on that network. Every device whose address starts with 192.168.30 is on the same subnet. A device at 192.168.10.57 is on a different one, even though it ends in the same number.

That split decides who can talk to whom:

  • Devices on the same subnet reach each other directly. On a flat home network, every device can see every other device's open ports.
  • Devices on different subnets need something to route between them, which is exactly where a firewall can sit and decide what is allowed.
  • Some traffic never crosses at all. A router does not forward multicast between subnets, which is why a phone on one network asking "is there a TV here?" never reaches a TV on another, and the cast button stays grey. Nothing is blocked; the question just never arrives.

The same notation appears on the gateway itself. When the firewall's interface is set to 192.168.30.1/24, that one line says both "my address is .1" and "everything in 192.168.30.x is on this interface".

The trap: one /24 for everything

The usual home network has one subnet behind the router. Your laptop, the smart plug, the TV, a visiting friend's phone and the Proxmox host all get an address from the same pool. The only firewall rule that matters is the one between the house and the internet: the front door is guarded while every interior door stands open.

That holds until something on the inside goes bad. Cheap smart-home gear often runs old software that rarely sees an update, a phone picks up a malicious app, a guest's laptop arrives already infected. On a flat /24, any of them can scan the subnet and find the Proxmox web interface, the NAS share or the printer with its default password.

The fix: one /24 per zone

Lock Down Your Home Network groups devices into five zones, each with its own VLAN and its own /24:

ZoneVLANSubnetFirewallDHCP range
Trusted10192.168.10.0/24.1.100 to .199
Servers20192.168.20.0/24.1static only
IoT30192.168.30.0/24.1.100 to .249
Guest40192.168.40.0/24.1.100 to .249
Management99192.168.99.0/24.1static only

Two conventions make this plan easy to live with:

  • The third number matches the VLAN ID. When you see 192.168.30.57 in a log, you know it is an IoT device without looking anything up.
  • The firewall is always .1. Every zone's gateway is the same last number, so there is nothing to remember per network.

In OPNsense, each VLAN becomes its own interface with a static address and the right prefix, for example 192.168.30.1/24. A new interface allows nothing by default: OPNsense blocks traffic arriving on an interface with no pass rules, so each new network stays dark until you write its rules. That is the right starting point.

Resist making more zones on day one. Every zone is another rule set to write, test and keep tidy; add a sixth only when you can name the rule that would be different for it.

Smaller version: a servers /24 behind OPNsense

If you are not ready for VLANs yet, Homelab the Right Way starts with a single separate network for your servers, 10.30.0.0/24, on a Linux bridge on the Proxmox host. Add the bridge in /etc/network/interfaces and apply it with ifreload -a:

auto vmbr1
iface vmbr1 inet manual
    bridge-ports none
    bridge-stp off
    bridge-fd 0

Give the OPNsense VM a NIC on vmbr1 and assign it as SERVERS with the static address 10.30.0.1/24. Static IPs are recommended for servers, so they have predictable addresses. Then move one container at a time, giving it an address inside the new /24 and OPNsense as its gateway:

pct set 120 --net0 name=eth0,bridge=vmbr1,ip=10.30.0.20/24,gw=10.30.0.1
pct exec 120 -- sh -c 'ip route; ping -c2 10.30.0.1'

Notice that ip=10.30.0.20/24 carries the /24 too: it tells the container which addresses are local and which must go through the gateway.

Before you begin, write a table of old IP to new IP, and either keep the old address as a secondary for a while or update DNS and reverse proxy entries in the same sitting.

Don't forget the route back

A new subnet is invisible to the rest of the house until something knows how to reach it. Clients on the house LAN need a route to 10.30.0.0/24. The clean way is a static route on the house router: 10.30.0.0/24 via 192.168.10.2, the OPNsense WAN address. Then allow the house LAN in on OPNsense's WAN interface for the specific ports you need, and disable Block private networks on WAN, since in this layout your "WAN" is itself a private network.

Keep your management path where it is: leave the Proxmox web UI and SSH reachable on the house LAN, so a firewall mistake never locks you out of the host.

Checklist: planning your /24s

  • You can read any address in your logs and say which network it belongs to
  • Every device is listed with the zone it belongs in
  • One VLAN ID and one /24 per zone, with the third number matching the VLAN ID
  • The firewall is .1 on every network, set with the right prefix (e.g. 192.168.30.1/24)
  • Servers use static addresses; DHCP ranges are set only where a zone needs them
  • An old IP to new IP table is written before anything moves
  • The house router has a static route to the servers subnet
  • The Proxmox web UI and SSH stay reachable on the house LAN

item.content:encoded:
This blog now publishes a new article almost every day, the YouTube channel posts a video a day, and the podcast just launched. That is a lot to keep up with, so there is now one place that collects it: a free weekly email, every Sunday at 9 AM Eastern.

Sign up on the newsletter page, or use the form at the top or bottom of any post.

What is in each issue

  • The week's new articles. Proxmox, OPNsense, Home Assistant, backups, ZFS and self-hosting, each with a one-line summary so you can skip what you don't need.
  • The new videos. The week's YouTube videos and Shorts, once they are public.
  • The new podcast episode. The Homelab the Right Way Podcast publishes on Sundays; the issue links the episode and its show notes.
  • One tip from the books. A single check you can do in a few minutes, with the chapter it comes from.

Here is the kind of tip an issue carries, from Homelab the Right Way, chapter 1: set one Proxmox backup job to "All guests" with excludes instead of a hand-picked list. A VM added last week is then already covered, while a list you have to remember to edit is how new guests silently go unbacked.

Your welcome gift

After you confirm your email, the welcome page has two things waiting:

  • The one-page Homelab checklist: twelve checks taken from the chapter checklists in the books, covering backups, the cluster, the network and storage. Print it and tick it off.
  • A free sample chapter of every ebook.

How it works

  1. Enter your email on the newsletter page or in any post.
  2. Tap the link in the confirmation email. Nothing is sent until you confirm.

The newsletter is free and written with AI help, based on the Homelab the Right Way books, the same as this blog.

item.description: The Amazon tech products that keep going viral and keep selling for years: network switches, portable SSDs, power banks, smart plugs, cable management, mini PCs and more, picked for a homelab and home-office audience. Updated as new product videos go up.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The links on this page go to Amazon; buying through them supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

This is the running list behind our product Shorts and TikToks: tech that keeps going viral AND has kept selling well for years, filtered for a homelab, desk-setup and smart-home audience. Each one got its own short video with a fictional AI presenter (the presenter is AI-generated; we do not claim to have personally tested these). No prices or ratings here because they change weekly; check the listing.

1. TP-Link TL-SG105 5-port gigabit switch

The first upgrade almost every homelab makes: one cable from the router gives you four more full-speed gigabit ports for the server, NAS, Pi and desktop. Metal case, fanless, nothing to configure. See it on Amazon

2. SanDisk 2TB Extreme Portable SSD

A pocket solid-state drive with no moving parts, USB-C, rated for drops and splashes, fast enough that a full laptop or VM backup takes minutes. See it on Amazon

3. INIU 10,000 mAh 45W power bank

Jacket-pocket size, 45 W over USB-C (enough for a USB-C laptop, tablet or Steam Deck), a short built-in detachable cable plus a USB-A port, flight-safe capacity. See it on Amazon

4. Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini EP10 (2-pack)

A Wi-Fi plug with no hub and no subscription: hard-reboot a frozen mini PC or router from your phone, schedule desk lights, works with Alexa, Google Home and Home Assistant. See it on Amazon

5. Alex Tech 10 ft split cable sleeve

Braided split tubing you push the cables into: ten seconds to a clean bundle behind a desk or under a rack shelf, cut to length, reusable, keeps pets off the cords. See it on Amazon

6. KAMRUI AK1PLUS mini PC (Intel N5095, 16 GB)

A palm-size, low-power desktop that is a popular first Proxmox or Home Assistant box: dual HDMI, 16 GB RAM, an M.2 SSD you can swap, and it sips power on a shelf 24/7. See it on Amazon

7. TP-Link Archer AX21 AX1800 Wi-Fi 6 router

The budget Wi-Fi 6 router that shows up in every "what router should I buy" thread: dual-band, gigabit ports, OneMesh, and it runs as a plain access point behind an OPNsense box. See it on Amazon

8. Anker 8-in-1 USB-C docking station

One cable from the laptop to two monitors, Ethernet, USB-A ports and power delivery; the desk dock people keep recommending for hybrid work setups. See it on Amazon

9. Govee 16.4 ft RGBIC LED strip

The strip behind half the desk and rack photos online: segment colours, app and voice control, music sync, and it is the Govee line Home Assistant users pick. See it on Amazon

10. Anker 2100J surge-protector power strip

A flat-plug surge protector with a 2100-joule rating, multiple outlets and USB ports: the strip to put under a desk full of chargers and small boxes. See it on Amazon

11. Amazon Smart Plug

The plug that makes any lamp, fan or coffee maker voice-controlled through Alexa, with no hub to buy: it sets up from the Alexa app in minutes, runs timers, schedules and routines, and reconnects on its own after a power or Wi-Fi outage. The compact shape leaves the second outlet free. See it on Amazon

12. Seagate 2TB portable hard drive

A plug-and-play USB 3.0 drive for Windows or Mac with 2 TB of space and no software to install: connect it, drag and drop, and the backup is done. It ships with an 18-inch USB 3.0 cable and is the drive people grab for a cheap offsite copy of their homelab backups. See it on Amazon

13. Syntech USB-C to USB adapter (2-pack)

Two small zinc-alloy adapters that turn a USB-C or Thunderbolt port into a USB 3.0 Type-A port, rated for 10,000 plug cycles, plug and play with no driver. They work with modern MacBooks, iPhones with USB-C and most USB-C laptops, tablets and phones, and come in a small foam case. See it on Amazon

14. WD 2TB Elements portable hard drive

Western Digital's plug-and-play portable drive with 2 TB in a small, light enclosure over SuperSpeed USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps), for PC and Mac, with a USB 3.0 cable in the box. The Elements line goes up to 6 TB if you want a bigger one for the same job. See it on Amazon

15. Jadaol 50 ft flat Cat6 Ethernet cable with clips

A flat, white 50-foot Cat6 patch cable rated to 250 MHz and 10 Gbps, with gold-plated RJ45 ends and bare-copper conductors, that runs along baseboards, around corners or under a carpet and comes with clips to pin it in place. The cable for the room the Wi-Fi never quite reaches. See it on Amazon

16. SanDisk 128GB Ultra Dual Drive (USB-C and USB-A)

A 128 GB flash drive with two retractable connectors, a reversible USB-C plug on one end and a standard USB-A plug on the other, so the same stick moves files between a phone, a tablet and a computer without an adapter. USB 3.1 Gen 1 with read speeds up to 150 MB/s, and SanDisk's Memory Zone app for Android manages and backs up phone content onto it. See it on Amazon

17. QINLIANF 5-outlet wall extender with 4 USB ports

A surge-protecting outlet extender that screws onto a standard duplex wall outlet: five AC outlets on three sides spaced 2.1 inches apart, plus three USB-A ports and one USB-C port with automatic charging detection, and 1,680 joules of surge protection with a "Protected" indicator light. ETL certified; it fits duplex outlets only, not GFCI. See it on Amazon

18. Logitech MK270 wireless keyboard and mouse combo

A full-size wireless keyboard with number pad, F-keys and eight multimedia hotkeys, paired with a compact ambidextrous mouse over one USB receiver with a range up to 33 feet. Spill-resistant design, adjustable tilt legs, and Logitech rates the batteries at 36 months for the keyboard and 12 months for the mouse, with on/off switches on both. See it on Amazon

19. Miady 2-pack 10,000 mAh slim power banks

Two slim 10,000 mAh power banks (one black, one white) with two USB-A ports and a bidirectional USB-C port, so each can charge up to three devices at once and recharges through the same USB-C port. Each measures about 5.5 by 2.6 by 0.6 inches and weighs about 7.7 ounces; two USB-C cables are in the box. See it on Amazon

20. Anker USB-C to USB-C cable, 60W, 6 ft (2-pack)

Two 6-foot braided-nylon USB-C to USB-C cables rated for 60 W Power Delivery charging and 480 Mbps data, with a core Anker rates for 5,000 bends and a hook-and-loop tie on each. USB-C only: no Lightning and no video output, which is exactly the cable you want for laptops, mini PCs, phones and tablets around the desk. See it on Amazon

21. HANYCONY 8-outlet surge protector power strip with 4 USB

A compact power strip with eight AC outlets across three sides, spaced 2.2 inches apart so bulky adapters do not block each other, plus two USB-A and two USB-C charging ports (5 V). It has a 5-foot braided cord with a flat right-angle plug, 1,080 joules of surge protection, a lit on/off switch with an integrated circuit breaker, and two keyhole slots for wall mounting. ETL and RoHS certified, rated 1875 W / 15 A. See it on Amazon

22. UGREEN Cat 8 braided Ethernet cable, 6 ft

A 6-foot Cat 8 patch cable rated for 40 Gbps and 2,000 MHz, built with four foil-shielded twisted pairs (F/FTP), pure copper 26 AWG conductors and gold-plated RJ45 plugs inside a cotton braided jacket UGREEN rates for 10,000 bends. PoE is supported and it is backward compatible with Cat 7, Cat 6 and Cat 5e gear. Most home equipment runs at 1 to 10 Gbps, so the shielding and durability are the practical gains, not the headline speed. See it on Amazon

23. havit HV-F2056 laptop cooling pad

A slim USB-powered cooling pad for 15.6 to 17-inch laptops with three quiet fans under a metal mesh deck, two adjustable height settings so it doubles as a stand, a power switch and an extra USB port. It measures about 15 by 11 by 1.2 inches. The included cable is USB-A, so a USB-C-only laptop needs a small adapter. See it on Amazon

24. Delamu cord hider raceway kit, 157 in

A wall cable raceway kit with 157 inches (13.1 feet) of pre-sectioned channel, 0.95 inches wide by 0.55 inches tall, that holds two to four cables under a snap-on, snap-off cover. It mounts with adhesive or screws, cuts to length, can be painted to match the wall, and ships with matching connectors and corner pieces; the PVC carries a UL94 V-0 flame-retardancy rating. The usual fix for the cables hanging under a wall-mounted TV. See it on Amazon

25. Logitech G305 Lightspeed wireless gaming mouse

A compact wireless gaming mouse with Logitech's HERO optical sensor (up to 12,000 DPI, 400 IPS) and LIGHTSPEED wireless at a 1 ms report rate, weighing 3.4 ounces. It runs about 250 hours on a single AA battery, or up to nine months in Endurance mode set through Logitech G HUB, has six buttons on an ambidextrous shape, and the nano receiver stores inside the mouse. See it on Amazon

26. NETGEAR GS305 5-port Gigabit Ethernet switch

A five-port unmanaged switch with 1 Gbps on every port, auto-negotiation that picks the right speed for each device, and support for the Cat5e or Cat6 cables you already have. It is plug-and-play with no software or setup, runs silent with no fan, uses IEEE 802.3az Energy Efficient Ethernet to cut power draw, and its compact metal case sits on a desk or mounts on a wall. The quick fix when the router runs out of ports. See it on Amazon

27. UGREEN 5-in-1 USB-C hub with 4K HDMI and 100W PD

A pocket USB-C adapter that adds a 4K HDMI output, a USB-C Power Delivery input that passes up to 100W through to the laptop, one 5 Gbps USB-A data port and two 480 Mbps USB-A ports. Handy for thin laptops with only one or two USB-C ports: a monitor, a charger, a keyboard, a mouse and a flash drive all hang off a single port. See it on Amazon

28. INIU 20,000 mAh pocket power bank with built-in cable

A compact 20,000 mAh power bank (about 11 ounces) that INIU rates for roughly four full phone charges, with 22.5W fast charging, a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a woven nylon lanyard, extra ports for other cables, and a small built-in flashlight. Its capacity is within the airline carry-on limit, and INIU backs it with a 3-year replacement warranty. See it on Amazon

29. Tapo C100 1080p indoor Wi-Fi camera

TP-Link's small plug-in indoor camera records 1080p Full HD with 850 nm infrared night vision up to 40 feet, person and motion detection with custom activity zones, baby-crying detection, and two-way audio with a built-in siren. Privacy mode pauses recording and privacy zones block out parts of the room. Video saves to a microSD card up to 512 GB or to the optional Tapo Care cloud. See it on Amazon

30. BESIGN LS03 aluminum laptop stand

A detachable aluminum laptop riser for 10 to 15.6-inch laptops that lifts the screen about 6 inches toward eye level, holds up to 8.8 lbs, and grips the laptop on rubber pads so it doesn't slide or scratch. The open frame lets air flow under the laptop, it assembles in three steps, and it comes apart flat for a bag or a drawer. See it on Amazon

31. Govee H6008 smart color light bulbs, 4-pack

Four A19 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LED bulbs on a standard E26 base, each putting out 800 lumens at 9 watts, with 16 million colors and 54 preset scenes. They take voice commands through Alexa and Google Assistant, run on timers and Sunrise and Sunset schedules from the Govee Home app, group with other Govee devices, and can change color with music picked up by your phone's microphone. They need a 2.4 GHz network and are not meant for use with smart wall switches. See it on Amazon

32. Samsung BAR Plus 128 GB USB 3.1 flash drive

A 128 GB USB-A flash drive in a metal body with a built-in keyring loop. Samsung rates it waterproof, shock-proof, temperature-proof, magnet-proof and X-ray-proof, backs it with a 5-year limited warranty, and says a 3 GB 4K video moves to a PC in about 10 seconds. A sturdy stick for a bootable installer or an offline copy of your configs. See it on Amazon

33. Tapo C210 2K pan/tilt indoor camera

TP-Link's indoor camera records 2K video and pans 360 degrees and tilts 114 degrees, so one camera can sweep a whole room. It sends alerts for motion, people and a crying baby, has two-way audio with a built-in siren and night vision up to 30 feet, and records to a microSD card up to 512 GB with no subscription, or to the optional Tapo Care cloud. It needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and works with Alexa and Google Assistant displays. See it on Amazon

34. TP-Link UB500 Bluetooth 5.4 USB adapter

A nano-sized USB dongle that adds Bluetooth 5.4 to a Windows PC, backward compatible with older Bluetooth versions and supporting both EDR and Bluetooth Low Energy for headsets, controllers, phones and printers. It is plug and play on Windows 10 and 11 (Windows 7 needs a free driver from TP-Link) and does not support macOS, Linux or TVs. TP-Link's tip: turn off any built-in Bluetooth in Device Manager first to avoid driver conflicts. See it on Amazon

35. D-Line 6 ft floor cord cover

A flexible PVC floor cable protector, 2.4 inches wide and 0.44 inches tall, that covers up to two cables of about 0.31 inches across in its inner channel. It ships coiled but lies flat, cuts to length with a utility knife or heavy-duty scissors, and its ribbed non-slip base and split back mean no tape is needed. Made for the cord that runs across a walkway to the desk or the rack. See it on Amazon

36. Anker Zolo 10,000 mAh 30W power bank

A pocket power bank, 4.32 x 2.58 x 0.98 inches, with a 5.4-inch USB-C cable built in that Anker says is tested past 10,000 bends. It charges devices at up to 30W and refills itself at up to 20W, and Anker rates it at about two full charges for an iPhone 15. Handy for keeping a phone alive during a long rack session or a power cut. See it on Amazon

37. Nettbe reusable hook-and-loop cable ties, 60-pack

Sixty 6-inch nylon hook-and-loop straps that wrap bundles up to about 40 mm across and peel off again when you re-cable. Unlike zip ties they never need cutting, so the same strap can move from the desk to the rack to the garage. The cheapest way to tame the mess behind a switch or a TV. See it on Amazon

38. Kingston NV3 1 TB M.2 NVMe SSD

A single-sided M.2 2280 drive on PCIe 4.0 x4, rated by Kingston at up to 6,000 MB/s read and 4,000 MB/s write. It comes with Acronis cloning software for moving an existing system over, and a 5-year limited warranty. A fast boot or VM drive for a mini PC, laptop or Proxmox node. See it on Amazon

39. TP-Link Deco X55 AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 mesh, 3-pack

A Wi-Fi 6 mesh system that TP-Link rates for up to 6,500 square feet and up to 150 devices across the three units. Each unit has three gigabit Ethernet ports and supports wired Ethernet backhaul, any unit can act as the router, and setup runs through the Deco app. Basic network security, QoS and parental controls are included at no cost. See it on Amazon

40. Seagate IronWolf 8 TB NAS hard drive

A 3.5-inch SATA 6 Gb/s drive built for NAS boxes of up to 8 bays, with up to 256 MB of cache and a 1 million hour MTBF rating. IronWolf Health Management lets a supported NAS watch the drive's health, and it carries a 3-year limited warranty plus 3 years of Rescue data recovery service. A common pick for a home media or backup array. See it on Amazon

How we pick

A product makes this list when it sits near the top of its Amazon Best Sellers category, has a long record of reviews over several years, and is the kind of thing people in the homelab and desk-setup corners of YouTube, TikTok and Reddit keep making videos about. The list is refreshed as new videos go up; the newest picks are at the top of the channel's Shorts.

item.title: TP-Link TL-SG105: the 5-port gigabit switch most homelabs start with
item.description: What the TP-Link TL-SG105 unmanaged 5-port gigabit switch does, where it fits in a homelab, and what it does not do. With the short video and the Amazon link.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The Amazon link on this page supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

Get it on Amazon: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Switch

The short video on this page uses a fictional AI-generated presenter (AI face, voice and lip-sync). We have not personally tested this switch; the details below come from TP-Link's own product information. No price or rating is quoted because both change; check the listing.

The problem it solves

Most home routers have four Ethernet ports on the back. A homelab fills them fast: a server or mini PC, a NAS, a Raspberry Pi, a desktop. A small unmanaged switch fixes that with one cable: plug one of its ports into the router and the other four become extra wired ports on the same network.

What it is

  • 5 gigabit Ethernet ports (10/100/1000 Mbps, auto-negotiation on every port)
  • Metal case, no fan, so it is silent
  • Unmanaged and plug-and-play: no app, no web page, nothing to configure
  • Energy-efficient design, which matters for a box that runs 24/7 on a shelf
  • Sits on a desk or mounts on a wall
  • Works behind any router, including an OPNsense or pfSense box

Where it fits in a homelab

  • Under the desk: one cable from the router, four wired devices next to you.
  • Next to the server shelf: the mini PC running Proxmox, the NAS and the Pi all get wired gigabit links instead of Wi-Fi.
  • Behind the TV: a console, a streaming box and a smart TV on one wall jack.

What it does not do

It is unmanaged, so there are no VLANs, no port settings and no traffic graphs. If you want to split IoT devices onto their own VLAN, you need a managed or "easy smart" switch instead (TP-Link sells those under other model numbers). If you only need more ports, unmanaged is simpler and there is nothing to misconfigure. There is also an 8-port version if five is not enough.

item.title: SanDisk 2TB Extreme Portable SSD: the pocket backup drive that replaced spinning disks
item.description: What the SanDisk Extreme Portable SSD (2TB) is, where it fits for backups and a homelab, and what it does not replace. With the short video and the Amazon link.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The Amazon link on this page supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

Get it on Amazon: SanDisk 2TB Extreme Portable SSD

The short video for this product uses a fictional AI-generated presenter (AI face, voice and lip-sync). We have not personally tested this drive; the details below come from SanDisk's own product information. No price or rating is quoted because both change; check the listing.

The problem it solves

A lot of desks still back up to a spinning USB hard drive: slow, heavy, and one bad drop away from losing everything on it. A portable SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster and much harder to break in a bag.

What it is

  • Solid-state, no moving parts
  • USB-C, USB 3.2 Gen 2
  • Read speeds up to 1050 MB/s (SanDisk's figure)
  • Up to 3-meter drop protection and IP65 water and dust resistance
  • 256-bit AES hardware encryption with password protection
  • Pocket-size, with a carabiner loop to clip it to a bag
  • Also sold in 1TB and 4TB

Where it fits

  • The "1" in 3-2-1: a copy of your photos, documents or VM backups that lives somewhere other than the machine it came from.
  • Moving big files: a full laptop image or a stack of VM exports in minutes instead of an evening.
  • Travel: a backup copy that rides along without worrying about bumps.

What it does not do

One drive is not a backup strategy on its own. If it is your only copy, it is a single point of failure like any other disk. Keep at least one more copy somewhere else, and test a restore now and then. The book Never Lose Your Data walks through the whole 3-2-1 setup.

The podcast launched last night (episode 1: The green check lies), and a few lines from it deserved to be printed. Seven new designs are in the Homelab the Right Way merch store today: two tees, a hoodie, an embroidered dad hat, a mug and two stickers. Same rules as every drop: original typography, printed or embroidered to order by Printful, nothing sitting in a warehouse. The hosts, Maya, Sam and Theo, are fictional AI hosts, so none of them appear on anything; the show's rack-and-mics logo does.

The Green Check Lies (tee)

The Green Check Lies Tee: a teal check box, the three words that open the first episode, and the pill underneath, "Backed up is not the same as restored." The green check on a Proxmox backup job proves the job ran. It does not prove the archive restores, that new VMs were included, or that the retention policy kept anything. item.content:encoded:
The Homelab the Right Way Podcast is here. Three hosts, Maya, Sam and Theo, talk through what the blog and the books keep coming back to: backups you can actually restore, networks that fail safe, self-hosting without the classic traps, and the small hardware details that quietly ruin a weekend.

A note on the hosts: Maya, Sam and Theo are fictional AI hosts. Their voices are synthetic, their faces in the clips are generated, and the episode was written with AI and edited by a human. Every fact in the episode comes from the Homelab the Right Way books and the posts linked below, so if something sounds too good to be true, the source is one tap away.

Chapters

  • 00:04 — Cold open and welcome
  • 02:39 — Backups: the green check lies
  • 14:36 — Storage: RAID is not a backup, the NFS trap, and ZFS done right
  • 19:39 — Gear break: the first switch
  • 21:09 — Networking: what a /24 means and why your 2-node cluster freezes
  • 27:04 — Self-hosting your photos, files and passwords the safe way
  • 32:43 — Home Assistant: the motion light that turns off on you, and the Zigbee fix
  • 36:17 — Gear break: the smart plug that reboots things
  • 37:36 — The turtle tank: the wire that fries an ESP32, and the sensor that lies
  • 44:29 — Three things we'd tell a beginner, and where to find all of this

What the episode covers, with the articles

Backups (02:39). The green check on a Proxmox backup job proves the job wrote some bytes somewhere, nothing more. The hosts walk through the 3-2-1 plan, keep-daily=7 and why it is not seven days of history, the backup job that silently skips every guest you created after you made it, Proxmox Backup Server on its own hardware, the four restore drills, the notification system and the dead-man's switch for jobs that stop running.

  • Proxmox backups that actually work: 3-2-1, step by step
  • keep-daily=7 doesn't mean 7 days of backups
  • Your Proxmox backup job is probably skipping your new VMs
  • A backup job that never runs never fails

Storage (14:36). The NFS share that drops at boot and lets a backup job fill the hypervisor's root disk, and the two-word fix (is_mountpoint). Why RAID and ZFS mirrors are one copy on resilient disks, why snapshots die with the pool, and the sanoid + syncoid pull-replication setup with a monthly checksum restore.

  • When your NFS share drops, Proxmox backups fill your root disk
  • RAID is not a backup: the 3-2-1 rule, honestly
  • Snapshots on a schedule, replicas on another box: sanoid and syncoid pull replication for ZFS

Networking (21:09). What the /24 after an address actually says, why one flat network for the whole house is the trap, the five-zone plan from Lock Down Your Home Network, and why a two-node Proxmox cluster freezes the moment one node goes down (one vote out of two is not more than half). The QDevice fix, the Wi-Fi trap and the pvecm expected 1 emergency lever.

  • What a /24 subnet actually means
  • Why your 2-node Proxmox cluster freezes

Self-hosting (27:04). Immich, Nextcloud or Syncthing, and Vaultwarden on one small box, and the six traps around them: one disk for everything, the Immich database on a network share, the hand-built Nextcloud, open signups and plain HTTP on Vaultwarden, forwarding ports to everything, and the backup that isn't one.

  • Self-host your photos, files and passwords the safe way

Home Assistant (32:43). The motion light that turns off while you are still in the hallway (mode: single is the culprit; mode: restart plus a wait_for_trigger with a for: is the fix), and the Zigbee fix that beats any setting: the coordinator on a USB 2.0 extension cable, away from the case and the access point.

  • New book: Automations That Just Work (Home Assistant without the surprises)

The turtle tank (37:36). The Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 water monitor from Smart Turtle Tank: the one wire that can fry the board (the turbidity sensor's 4.5 V output into a 3.3 V pin, and the voltage divider that fixes it), the DS18B20 readings of 85 °C and -127 °C that are not temperatures at all, and the three numbers a tank has to get right before any electronics go near it.

  • The one wire that can fry your ESP32 tank monitor
  • DS18B20 reads 85 °C or -127 °C? Here's why
  • 3 numbers your turtle tank has to get right

Gear mentioned in this episode

  • Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini EP10 (2-pack): a Wi-Fi plug with no hub and no subscription. Hard-reboot a frozen mini PC or router from your phone, and it works with Home Assistant.

The problem it solves

Every homelab has one box that hangs: the cheap mini PC, the old router, the Raspberry Pi with the flaky SD card. When it locks up, the fix is pulling the power cord. A Wi-Fi smart plug turns that into a tap in an app, from the couch or from anywhere.

What it is

  • A Wi-Fi plug on 2.4 GHz, no hub needed
  • On and off from the Kasa app, at home or away
  • Schedules, timers and an away mode
  • Works with Alexa and Google Home
  • Home Assistant has an integration for Kasa devices
  • Ultra-mini size, so two fit in one outlet
  • Sold as a 2-pack

Where it fits

  • Remote hard reboot: put the box that freezes behind one and power-cycle it when it stops answering.
  • Schedules: desk lights, a monitor, or a test box that only needs to run in the evening.
  • Home Assistant: automate it with everything else, for example cut power to a hung device after a ping check fails (do this with care; see below).

What it does not do

A smart plug cuts power hard; it does not shut a machine down cleanly. Do not use one to switch off a NAS or a server in the middle of writes, and never put it in front of the device that runs your network or your Home Assistant, or you lose the way to turn it back on. Use it for things that are safe to yank, and keep a proper shutdown for anything with data on it. Plugs on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi also depend on your Wi-Fi being up.

The problem it solves

Most small power banks top up a phone and nothing else. Plug a USB-C laptop or a handheld into one and the battery level barely moves, because the bank cannot push enough watts. This one puts out up to 45 W over USB-C in a jacket-pocket size.

What it is

  • 10,000 mAh capacity, roughly two full phone charges
  • Up to 45 W over USB-C
  • A short USB-C cable built in, and it detaches
  • A USB-A port for a second device
  • Recharges over the same USB-C port
  • Capacity under the usual airline carry-on battery limit
  • Multi-protection charging circuit (the maker's description)

Where it fits

  • USB-C laptops and tablets: 45 W is enough for a MacBook Air-class laptop or a tablet to gain charge, not just slow the drain.
  • Steam Deck and other handhelds: one bank, one cable, already attached.
  • The go-bag: a homelab person's travel kit usually has a laptop, a phone and a cable pile; this covers two of the three.

What it does not do

10,000 mAh is not a laptop's worth of battery. Expect a partial laptop top-up, not a full charge, and a big gaming laptop that wants 100 W or more will not run from it. If you need several full laptop charges, look at a bigger 20,000 to 25,000 mAh bank instead.
